summary: A request for comments about the procedure for updating the naming registry and distributing host tables, as it exists and as it might. None of the proposals are standards.

eli5.summary: How do you keep everyone's list of computer names up to date? This memo asks for ideas.

subtitle: A request for comments on how to improve the distribution and updating of host name tables across the Internet.

tldr.problem: The central NIC host table was the source of truth for Internet hostnames, but it was not reliable enough for sites to depend on. Each site had to maintain its own copy, and there was no good way to know when updates were available or to distribute them efficiently.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC proposes four approaches to improving host table distribution: (1) a push protocol with a registered port for sites to receive updates, (2) a version-checking protocol so sites can see if their copy is current, (3) email-based distribution, and (4) a combination of push on startup and periodic polling. The author prefers the combination approach.
tldr.outcome: This RFC remains a request for comments; none of these proposals became standards at the time. Modern Internet infrastructure uses DNS rather than centralized host tables, making the problem moot.

today: RFC 849 is an informational request for comments from 1983. The problems it describes were ultimately solved differently: the Internet adopted the Domain Name System (DNS), which uses distributed, hierarchical name servers rather than a single centralized host table. Modern DNS includes mechanisms for caching, updates, and redundancy that address all the concerns raised in this RFC.

sections.title: The Problem with Host Table Updates
sections.content:
In 1983, each Internet site was expected to maintain its own copy of the master HOSTS.TXT file from the NIC (SRI-NIC). However, SRI-NIC was not reliable enough to depend on as a live name server, so sites could not simply query it for each lookup. The NIC ran on Tenex and Foonly systems that, while serving internal NIC needs, lacked the high availability and performance required for a critical network service.

The NIC offered both a service to dump the entire name registry and anonymous FTP access to HOSTS.TXT, but someone at each site had to know to retrieve the latest version. The NIC did not reliably announce updates, and there was no automated way for a site to check whether its local copy was current.
sections.eli5: The NIC had the right list, but their computer was not fast enough to answer everyone. So everyone copied the list locally. But no one knew when the copy was out of date.

sections.title: Four Proposed Solutions
sections.content:
The author proposes four solutions, in order of increasing complexity and automation. Solution (1) is a new push protocol: a server process on each site listens on a registered port, and the NIC ships updates directly to registered sites, with a checksum to verify integrity. Solution (2) is a version-checking protocol where the NIC reports the current version of the host table, allowing sites to check if their copy is current without transferring the entire file.

Solution (3) uses email to mail updated host tables to a list of recipients, but the author notes this is impractical for large files. Solution (4) combines approaches (1) and (2): the NIC pushes updates to registered sites (trying once), and each site runs a program at startup and periodically (e.g., daily) to poll the NIC for possible updates as a backup mechanism.
sections.eli5: Option one: NIC sends you updates whenever it changes something. Option two: you call and ask if anything changed. Option three: it emails you (not great). Option four: it tries to send but you also call to check—the best plan.

sections.title: The Long-Term Solution
sections.content:
The author also notes that a longer-term solution would be to replace or augment the SRI-NIC system with reliable, dedicated VAX Unix systems offering a highly responsive name service. Such a service would eventually eliminate the need for sites to maintain local copies of the registry. However, this solution required money, time, and effort that might not be immediately available.

The RFC explicitly states that none of the proposed solutions are intended as standards at the time; rather, the hope is that discussion will lead to a general consensus on the appropriate solution. The document is a genuine request for comments from the community on the best path forward.
sections.eli5: The real fix might be to build a really reliable central name service so no one needs local copies. But that would take time and money. For now, the author asks everyone: which of these ideas is best?
